title: Are Marine Protected Areas an Effective Tool to Aid Recovery of Palinurus elephas (European Crawfish) in the North Atlantic?
content:
ABSTRACT

Crawfish (Palinurus elephas) were once common across rocky reefs in the North-East Atlantic, but during the 1980s widespread extirpation reduced the species to a few isolated populations in remote areas. Since 2010, the species has begun to recover and is now recolonizing much of its former range. Owing to its high commercial value, fisheries landings have increased 50% per year since 2019 leading to concerns of overexploitation. In the UK a key management measure is the designation of marine conservation zones (MCZs)—a spatial management tool through which regional fisheries authorities can impose fisheries prohibitions to protect populations. We combined data from multiple sources, including commercial catch recording and various tracking studies (mark recapture and acoustic telemetry) to conduct an integrated analysis of spatial ecology, assessing the efficacy of MCZs and provide broad-scale baseline data for further studies on population status. We found sex dependent movement characteristics with higher mobility of males during reproductive seasons. Ultimately, however, most individuals occupied small territories (~4 km2), with maximum dispersal distances ranging between 94 m and 4.6 km (1.6 ± 1.1 km—mean ± SD). A notable exception was observed in two subadults, which dispersed 164 and 165 km, suggestive that some individuals exhibit nomadic behaviour. While MCZs have strong potential to safeguard localized populations, they are not a complete solution. In particular, the species' reproductive strategy includes a long planktonic larval phase (~12 months), resulting in highly variable recruitment events that a static network of protected areas cannot reliably protect. Consequently, long-term population persistence will also depend on broad-scale monitoring of population processes and commercial fisheries effort.
